lines.text: Here's the whole trick. Photo one, from two meters, started our guess at x equals two point nine seven.
Photo two says three. How far should we move? The gain, K, decides: our variance, over our variance plus the photo's noise.
First, widen our guess a hair for two millimeters of drift. Its variance becomes zero point zero zero two zero three three.
Photo two is also from two meters. Its noise is zero point zero zero two zero three four. Almost the same.
So K is zero point five. Equal trust, so we move halfway.
New guess equals old guess, plus K times the difference. Two point nine seven, plus half of three centimeters: two point nine eight five.
The same for y, now zero point five eight five, and for heading, now one seventy nine point five degrees.
Then the variance shrinks, times one minus K. We're surer: sigma drops from four point five to three point two centimeters.
With equally sharp photos, this is the ordinary average. The first counts fully, the second gets a half, the third a third.
This smart average is called a Kalman filter. Ours is tiny: one for x, one for y, and one for heading.
